passage: Monday. After lunch, Vasudha, nine, left the school tap dribbling while she chatted with Parul. "One tap won't empty the tank," she said. Across the yard, other taps dribbled too. Wednesday. By the last period the tank was dry. Class 4 couldn't wash their tiffins, and the toilets smelled. The peon said every tap had been left open a little. Vasudha went quiet. She had thought it was only hers. Friday. Vasudha and Parul made signs in fat crayon: "Close me! Every drop is ours." They taped one above each tap. At break Vasudha caught herself about to walk away, and turned the tap off with a firm twist.

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Parul write on the signs?
qa.a: "Close me! Every drop is ours."

qa.q: Why did Vasudha go quiet on Wednesday?
qa.a: She realised her dribbling tap was one of many, and felt guilty for thinking only hers wouldn't matter.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha and Parul make on Friday, and why could it help?
qa.a: They taped signs above each tap, reminding everyone that every drop is shared, so each person turns the tap off.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Class 4?
qa.a: They couldn't wash their tiffins and had to put up with smelly toilets, paying for everyone's dribbling taps.

grounding: A girl leaves a school tap running, sure one tap cannot matter, until everyone doing the same empties the shared tank.

passage: Jeevan Dadu pointed his stick at the green pond. "Rashmi, when I was ten, you could see fish in that water. Every child in the village swam there after school. And every one of us threw our sugarcane peels and paper in it. I used to think, 'My peel is so small. What difference can it make?' Everybody thought the same. One summer the water turned green and smelly. The fish floated up, belly first. The panchayat closed the pond, and we had nowhere to swim. That summer was long and hot and sad. That's why I still pick up peels along the bank."

qa.q: What did the children throw into the pond?
qa.a: Sugarcane peels and paper.

qa.q: What did young Jeevan think about his own peel?
qa.a: He thought it was so small it couldn't make a difference.

qa.q: What choice does Jeevan make now because of that summer?
qa.a: He still picks up peels along the bank, having learned that everyone's small peels together ruined the pond.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see a single wrapper after hearing this story?
qa.a: Rashmi may see it as part of a pile made by everyone, not a harmless little thing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, he and every other child littered a village pond thinking one peel didn't matter, until it was spoiled.

passage: The colony had one good cricket bat, bought with everyone's pocket money, and dark clouds were rolling in. Jatin, eleven, got it first and wouldn't let go. "Just one more over. Then Ramesh." Ramesh waited. So did the others. When Jatin was finally out, Ramesh grabbed the bat and kept it just as long. Then the next kid did the same. Nobody passed it on. They yanked it back and forth, arguing, and it slipped onto the wet concrete in the first drops of rain. The handle cracked. They stood in the drizzle, staring at it. "I only kept it a bit," Jatin muttered. "So did we all," said Ramesh.

qa.q: How was the colony's cricket bat bought?
qa.a: With everyone's pocket money.

qa.q: What was Jatin thinking in muttering 'I only kept it a bit'?
qa.a: Jatin felt that one person's extra time was too small to be the cause, not seeing that everyone had thought the same.

qa.q: What could the children agree on to protect the next bat?
qa.a: A fixed number of overs each, with the bat passed on in turn, so no one needs to hog it.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's reply 'So did we all' show about how Ramesh sees what happened?
qa.a: Ramesh sees that each of them took a little extra, and together that spoiled the bat they all owned.

grounding: Children each hog a shared cricket bat a little, thinking one person's share doesn't matter, until the fighting over it breaks the bat.

passage: The Class 5 paint tubs were bought with everyone's craft fund. On Monday Yamini, ten, squeezed out a huge blob of blue for a tiny sky, and left the lid off. "There's loads," she told Vaibhav. "My little bit won't finish it." Vaibhav squeezed out red the same way. So did the table behind them. Nobody put lids back, because nobody thought one open tub mattered. By Thursday the blue had a hard, cracked crust. The yellow was dry as chalk. When Ms Pinto announced the Independence Day posters, there was almost no paint left. Yamini poked the crust with her brush and said nothing.

qa.q: What did the paint tubs look like by Thursday?
qa.a: The blue had a hard, cracked crust and the yellow was dry as chalk.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel about using the paint on Monday?
qa.a: She felt unconcerned, believing her little bit would not matter because there was loads of paint, so she did not bother with the lid.

qa.q: What could Yamini do differently with the next set of shared paints?
qa.a: She could squeeze out only what she needs and close the lid each time, and suggest the class does the same, since the paint belongs to everyone.

qa.q: How are the rest of the class affected when the posters are announced?
qa.a: Everyone, including children who were careful, now has almost no paint for the Independence Day posters, even though the craft fund was theirs too.

grounding: A ten-year-old wastes class paint thinking her share cannot matter, everyone does the same, and the shared paint is spoiled for all.

passage: "Nirmala! Why is there no water in the bathroom?" Mummy called. "The whole building's tank is empty." Nirmala, eleven, looked at her little brother Tenzin. Tenzin looked at the ceiling. "We were washing our cycles on the terrace," he said. "With the hose," Nirmala added. "Only for a bit." "How long is a bit?" "Maybe... an hour? The Mehtas' kids were also doing it. And the boys from the fourth floor were having a water fight." Mummy sat down. "So everyone thought their bit was small." "One hose can't empty a whole tank, Mummy." "Five hoses can." Tenzin whispered, "Mrs Rao can't cook now, can she?" Nirmala felt her face go hot. "We could carry her a bucket from the corner tap."

qa.q: What were Nirmala and Tenzin doing on the terrace?
qa.a: They were washing their cycles with the hose.

qa.q: How can you tell Nirmala feels guilty once Mummy points out the problem?
qa.a: Her face goes hot when Tenzin mentions Mrs Rao, and she quickly offers to carry a bucket to her.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene could change how the children use the terrace hose?
qa.a: The moment Mummy says five hoses can empty the tank shows them their bit was not small, so next time they could use a bucket and stop quickly.

qa.q: How are neighbours like Mrs Rao affected by what the children did?
qa.a: Mrs Rao cannot cook because the whole building's tank is empty, even though she had nothing to do with the hoses.

grounding: An eleven-year-old and other children each waste the building's shared water thinking one hose does not matter, and the tank runs dry for everyone.

passage:
Wednesday
Today I left the tap in the school ground running after I washed my tiffin. I thought, it's just one tap, and I was late for PT. Zeenat said she did the same yesterday. So did the boys from 5B.
After lunch there was no water at all. The whole tank was empty. Nobody could wash their hands. Ma'am said the tank fills only once a day, and today it ran out because taps were left open. The little kids from class one cried because they were thirsty.
I felt my face get hot. I didn't tell anyone it was me. But I kept thinking: if everyone thinks one tap doesn't matter, then every tap is left on.
Tomorrow I am going to close every tap I pass, even if it's not mine.
- Nirmala

qa.q: How often does the tank fill?
qa.a: The tank fills only once a day.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when the little kids cried?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and guilty, face getting hot, knowing that open tap was part of the problem.

qa.q: What small step does Nirmala plan, and why could it help?
qa.a: Nirmala plans to close every tap on the way, which could save water and show others that each person's choice matters.

qa.q: How might the class-one children experience the empty tank?
qa.a: They were thirsty and upset, suffering from a problem they didn't cause.

grounding: A child leaves a school tap running thinking one share doesn't matter, and when everyone does the same, the shared water runs out.

passage: Behind the temple in their village, the pond used to be where Hemant and his sister Swati caught tadpoles. This summer Hemant, eleven, tossed his chips packet in without thinking. Everyone did. The chai-stall owner threw paper cups; the older boys dumped their bottles after cricket. One packet can't hurt, Hemant told himself. By June the pond smelled like rotten eggs. A green scum covered the water, and the buffaloes wouldn't drink from it. Swati found a dead fish floating near the steps. "Who did this?" she asked. Hemant opened his mouth, then shut it. He remembered all the packets he had thrown. So had everyone else, probably. They stood on the stone steps, looking at the ruined pond, and he felt sick in his stomach.

qa.q: What did Swati find near the steps?
qa.a: Swati found a dead fish floating near the steps.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he looked at the ruined pond?
qa.a: Hemant felt guilty and sick, remembering all the packets he had thrown.

qa.q: What could Hemant and Swati do next?
qa.a: They could start by picking up the rubbish they see and ask the village elders to put a bin near the pond, so everyone has another choice.

qa.q: How does Swati see the pond compared to before?
qa.a: Swati is upset and shocked, remembering it as a place for tadpoles now spoiled by rubbish.

grounding: A child litters the shared village pond thinking one packet doesn't matter, and when everyone does the same the pond is spoiled.

passage: At Nour's school in Amman, there was one good football for the whole of year four. Nour, nine, always grabbed it first at break and kept it until the bell, even when others were waiting. Why not? Hana did the same when she got it first, and so did the boys from the other class. Everyone kicked it hard against the wall, left it out in the rain, and nobody ever returned it to the box. One Monday the ball came back flat, a split down the side. The PE teacher held it up. "This belonged to all of you. Now it belongs to none of you." Nour stared at the ground. Break that day was long and boring. Hana kicked a stone. "It wasn't only you," she said. "It was everyone." That didn't make Nour feel any better.

qa.q: What did the PE teacher say about the ball?
qa.a: The PE teacher said, "This belonged to all of you. Now it belongs to none of you."

qa.q: How did Nour feel when the teacher held up the flat ball?
qa.a: Nour felt ashamed and guilty, staring at the ground, knowing the hogging and rough use were partly Nour's doing.

qa.q: How could year four look after a new ball?
qa.a: They could agree on turns at break, and on returning the ball to the box, so everyone plays and it lasts.

qa.q: How does Hana see the blame for the ball?
qa.a: Hana feels it was everyone's fault, not only Nour's, which shows she knows she was part of the problem too.

grounding: A child hogs and misuses a shared football thinking one share doesn't matter; when everyone does the same, the ball is ruined.

passage:
The school had one big water tank on the roof and a row of taps near the playground. At lunch break, Salma turned a tap on full and splashed her face, then ran off to play hopscotch with the tap still gushing.
"Salma, your tap!" Irfan shouted, waving his arms.
"It's just one tap," she called back. "The tank is huge."
Other children did the same. Taps dripped and ran all through the break.
After the last period, Salma's water bottle was empty. She went to the taps. They coughed air. The peon said the tank was dry and the tanker would come only tomorrow. The toilets smelled bad by evening.

qa.q: What did the peon say about the tank?
qa.a: The peon said the tank was dry and the tanker would come only tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Salma think when she said, "It's just one tap"?
qa.a: She felt relaxed and unworried, sure that her one running tap could not matter because the tank was so big.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Every child thought one tap did not matter, so the tank emptied; closing each tap after use, and reminding each other, would keep water for everyone.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Salma's answer after the taps run dry?
qa.a: Irfan may feel frustrated, because he warned her and now the whole school has no water.

grounding: Illustrates a child leaving a school tap running because one share seems too small to matter, while everyone doing the same empties the shared tank.

passage:
Monday: Sudha finished her chips on the park bench and dropped the packet behind it. One wrapper, she thought. The park was big.
Thursday: Yogesh called her to play near the slide, but they had to step around cups, peels and packets. Someone had tipped a plate of leftover pav near the swings. Crows fought over it. "Everyone throws stuff here now," Yogesh said. Sudha noticed her own blue packet still behind the bench.
The next Sunday: the park smelled so bad that Yogesh's mother would not let him go. Sudha stood at the gate alone, looking at the swings. Then she went home, came back with an old bag, and picked up her blue packet first.

qa.q: What colour was Sudha's chips packet?
qa.a: Her packet was blue.

qa.q: What might Sudha be feeling when she spots her own blue packet behind the bench?
qa.a: She probably feels a sting of guilt, seeing that her one wrapper is part of the mess she is now stepping around.

qa.q: Which choice at the end could help the park, and why?
qa.a: Picking up her own packet first is a small start, and if she asks Yogesh and other children to join, the park could become usable again.

qa.q: What is it like for Yogesh when his mother will not let him go?
qa.a: Yogesh loses his play place and may feel disappointed, even though he was not the only one who spoiled it.

grounding: Shows a child littering a shared park on the idea that one wrapper does not matter, and the park being spoiled as everyone does the same.

passage:
Pranav, sit, I'll tell you about the bat. When I was ten, the whole village collected money for one real cricket bat. Willow, with a red grip. It lived in the panchayat room, for all of us boys.
And what did we do? I used it to hit stones into the pond. Just a few, I thought. Who would know? Gautam used it to knock mangoes off trees. Every boy had his own small misuse.
In one month the blade cracked right down the middle. No more cricket that summer. We played with a plank of wood and argued the whole time.
I still remember the day the crack came. It was my stone.

qa.q: What colour was the grip of the village bat?
qa.a: The bat had a red grip.

qa.q: What does the elder feel when saying, "It was my stone"?
qa.a: The elder still feels guilty and a little ashamed, knowing his own careless hits helped break the bat everyone shared.

qa.q: What choice could the boys have made when the bat first arrived?
qa.a: They could have agreed to use it only for cricket and to keep it in the panchayat room, so each boy guarded it instead of misusing it a little.

qa.q: How would Gautam have been affected when the bat cracked?
qa.a: Gautam lost his cricket too, and may have felt his own mango-knocking was part of the damage.

grounding: Shows a boy misusing a shared cricket bat because one person's small misuse seemed not to matter, until everyone's misuse broke it.

passage: It was Holi in a dry March, and the colony's overhead tank was half empty because the water tanker hadn't come for two days. Everyone knew. But the pichkari fight was on, and Pallavi kept running back to the common tap to refill, leaving it gushing while she shot at Pradeep. 'Close it!' Pradeep shouted. 'One tap won't matter,' she yelled back. A dozen other children were thinking the same thing at six other taps. By evening the tank was dry. Nobody could wash off the colour. Pallavi stood in the bathroom, green-faced and itchy, with an empty bucket, while her grandmother wiped her face with a mug of drinking water.

qa.q: Why was the overhead tank half empty?
qa.a: The water tanker hadn't come for two days.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when she said 'One tap won't matter'?
qa.a: Pallavi felt carefree and caught up in the fun, sure her own share was too small to matter.

qa.q: What could the children have agreed before the Holi fight?
qa.a: To fill buckets once and keep the taps closed, so the shared tank would last for washing afterwards.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when the tank runs dry?
qa.a: Pradeep would feel frustrated and annoyed, since he had warned Pallavi to close the tap.

grounding: During Holi a girl leaves a shared tap running, thinking her share doesn't matter, as everyone else does the same.

passage: During Ganesh Chaturthi the colony ground in Pune became a fair: stalls, lights and a hundred children eating vada pav. Vandana finished hers and dropped the paper plate by the swing. 'Dustbin's far,' she told Tanuja. 'Everyone does it.' Tanuja shrugged and dropped hers too. So did the boys by the slide, and the aunties by the stall. By the tenth day the ground where they played cricket every evening was carpeted with plates and cups, the swings smelled sour, and a stray dog had cut its paw on a broken cup. The colony secretary put up a notice: ground closed for cleaning, two weeks. Vandana stared at the chain across the gate. 'But it was just one plate,' she said.

qa.q: Where did Vandana drop her paper plate?
qa.a: By the swing.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel staring at the chain across the gate?
qa.a: Vandana feels shocked and a little guilty, realising her 'just one plate' added to the mess that closed the ground.

qa.q: What could the children do to keep the ground open next festival?
qa.a: Set up more bins near the swings and take turns reminding each other, so each small effort protects the shared ground.

qa.q: What would change if Tanuja had carried both plates to the dustbin?
qa.a: It might have nudged Vandana and others to do the same, so less rubbish would pile up.

grounding: During a festival a girl litters the shared ground believing one plate won't matter, until the ground is closed.

passage:
'Farida, it's been forty minutes. Give the bat,' Vishal called from the boundary.
'Two more overs!'
'You said that twenty minutes ago.'
'It's the common bat. It's for everyone.'
'Exactly! Everyone includes us.'
The winter camp had one good bat, the one with the blue grip, and every child wanted it. Farida swung again and hit the ball into the thorn bushes. When she finally handed the bat over, the blue grip was torn and the handle had a crack.
'Who did this?' Vishal said.
'Not me. It was already... maybe a bit.'
'Now nobody can use it properly.'
Farida looked at the crack. 'I thought one person using it more wouldn't matter.'
'Everybody thinks that,' Vishal said, and sighed.

qa.q: What colour was the grip on the good bat?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she looked at the crack?
qa.a: Farida felt guilty and uneasy, realising hogging the bat had helped ruin it for everyone.

qa.q: What rule could the camp make for the common bat?
qa.a: A fair turn system, such as two overs each, so nobody hogs it and it lasts longer.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel waiting at the boundary?
qa.a: Vishal feels impatient and frustrated, waiting forty minutes for a bat meant for everyone.

grounding: At a winter camp a girl hogs the shared cricket bat, thinking her extra use won't matter, until it cracks.

passage: Last summer, in the hottest week of May, our school tank ran dry on a Friday. I know part of why. Every break I let the tap by the playground run over my wrists to cool down, sometimes for five whole minutes. I thought, it's only me, it's one tap. But Sahil did it too. And the Class 6 kids filled bottles just to throw water at each other. On Friday there was no water for drinking or for the toilets, and Sister sent us all home early. Nobody cheered. Sahil nudged me. "Maria, that was us." My ears went hot, because I remembered every one of my five-minute splashes. Now I turn the tap off after one splash.

qa.q: On which day did the school tank run dry?
qa.a: On a Friday.

qa.q: Why did Maria's ears go hot on Friday?
qa.a: Maria felt guilty and embarrassed, remembering all the five-minute splashes that helped empty the tank.

qa.q: What could the school try so the tank lasts through summer?
qa.a: It could show every class how the whole tank depends on each tap, and put up simple reminders to turn taps off after one splash.

qa.q: What would change if only Maria had left the tap running?
qa.a: The tank might have lasted, but because Sahil and the Class 6 kids thought the same way, everyone's small waste added up.

grounding: A child lets the shared school tap run, thinking one person does not matter, and the tank runs dry because everyone thought the same.
